title: The Mellotron
hook: Each key plays a strip of real tape, so no note can last past eight seconds.
peek: The Mellotron looks like an organ but works like a shelf of tape recorders. Every key starts its own short recording of a real flute, violin or choir, and after about eight seconds the tape simply runs out.
lede: Long before digital samplers, the Mellotron offered real orchestral sounds at the touch of a key. Under each key sits a strip of magnetic tape holding a recording of an actual instrument playing that note. Press the key and a pinch roller pulls the tape across a playback head. Hold it for more than about eight seconds and the sound stops: the tape has reached its end.

bullets.text: When you let go of a key, a spring pulls its strip back to the start, ready for the next note. This is why Mellotron players learned to shift chords before the tapes ran out.

The idea came from the American inventor Harry Chamberlin, who built tape-based keyboards in the 1950s. The Bradley brothers in Birmingham, England, developed their own version, and the Mellotron went on sale in the early 1960s.

The soft, wobbly flute sound that opens the Beatles' 1967 song is a Mellotron. Groups such as the Moody Blues and King Crimson leaned on its strings and choirs to sound orchestral without hiring an orchestra.

Because each note is a physical tape, pitch drifts slightly and attack varies from key to key. Players once called this a flaw, but that unsteady, breathy quality is exactly what fans now love about it.
